problems.description: Greenfield commit ships +1363 lines across 9 files with zero tests, so nothing exercises the registry, message routing, or health endpoint
SUPPORTED_TYPES is duplicated in both Message and MessageHandler; a single constant should be the source of truth
Message.from_json performs no validation even though MessageHandler.validate_message exists, so a malformed frame yields a Message with type=None rather than being rejected
Measured cognitive complexity +45 across only 7 functions indicates handle_client/message routing is doing too much per function and could be decomposed

Measured convention score (0.77) is dragged down by apparent analyzer noise: flags reference app.py which is not in this commit and 'module-level constants' SUPPORTED_TYPES which is already UPPER_CASE, and __init__.py contains no function definitions; real violations are limited to self.type shadowing the type builtin and a message_type->type attribute naming mismatch
RLock-based thread safety in ClientRegistry is arguably unnecessary inside an asyncio single-threaded server, though harmless and defensive

strengths: Clean layered separation of concerns (ClientRegistry / MessageHandler / NotificationServer) that matches a microservices-compatible notification design
Thread-safe registry with a concise, well-documented API and snapshot returns that avoid lock-held exposure
Consistent docstrings and type hints across all modules
WS (8765) and REST health (8080) split with registry-backed health reporting follows standard service patterns
Message serialization path (to_json/from_json) is clean and matches the wire format used by the example client
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, well-modularized greenfield WebSocket notification server whose architecture fits the microservices story intent, but it ships with no tests and minor duplication/validation gaps, and the 0.77 convention measurement understates real adherence because the analyzer flagged spurious violations (app.py not in this diff, already-uppercase constants).

problems.description: ClientRegistry.unregister/disconnect is not updated to remove clients from _channels on websocket close, so disconnected clients leave stale IDs in channel sets — a slow memory leak and inflated get_active_channels/get_channel_subscribers counts. The `if cid in self._clients` guard in get_clients_in_channel masks the bug for broadcasts but does not fix the lifecycle gap.

SonarQube delta shows +21 cognitive complexity and +3 smells for a small feature; the branch in _broadcast_message (channel vs global) plus four new handlers add conditional surface that could be simplified (e.g., routing broadcast by explicit channel field rather than payload sniffing).
Tests cover subscribe/unsubscribe and channel-scoped broadcast but no case verifying that a disconnecting client is purged from its channel subscriptions.

Computed convention score 0.77 is codebase-wide and driven mostly by pre-existing violations in files this commit does not touch (__init__.py, app.py, example_usage.py); the diff's own additions are convention-clean, so the 0.77 understates the delta's compliance.

strengths: Feature fits the domain (channel/topic notifications) and is backward compatible: broadcast without a channel still reaches all clients.

Closely mirrors existing patterns — lock-protected state in ClientRegistry, the Message.type dispatch chain in NotificationServer, and the established async test fixture in test_notification_server.py.
New public methods carry type hints and docstrings consistent with project conventions.
Robust input handling: subscribe/unsubscribe with a missing channel are logged and skipped instead of raising.
Every new registry method is actually consumed (REST handlers and broadcast routing), no dead code.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-tested channel-subscription feature that faithfully extends the existing ClientRegistry/dispatch patterns and stays backward compatible, though it introduces debt by never purging channel subscriptions on client disconnect and adds moderate cognitive complexity.

problems.description: get_messages() and get_message_count() silently swallow exceptions and return empty/0, masking real failures at the storage layer
get_messages() duplicates the full SQL query and row-mapping loop across the channel/non-channel branches (consistent with the measured +1.7% duplication delta)
No context manager or finally around connections; conn.close() is skipped on the error paths in store_message/get_messages/clear_messages, leaking file handles when sqlite raises
Modified example_usage.py still carries PascalCase class / UPPER_CASE-constant violations flagged by the convention scan (score 0.77), though the new code in message_persistence.py itself is clean
datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and each operation opens a fresh connection with no WAL or pool; acceptable for low concurrency but not robust for the notification server's write path

strengths: MessagePersistence is a cohesive single-responsibility module cleanly separated from the server and handler layers, fitting the integration goal of Session 3
All SQL is parameterized, avoiding injection and keeping payloads JSON-encoded consistently
Every public method has a docstring, typed signatures, and logging on failures
Index on (channel, timestamp) backs the new query paths, and example_usage.py was extended to demonstrate the new read endpoints
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, idiomatic persistence layer that fits the integration phase and follows conventions in its own module, but it carries minor-to-major debt from duplicated SQL, silent error swallowing, and non-context-managed connections that inflate the measured complexity (+76) and smells (+3).

problems.description: Transport constructors receive both `client_registry` and server callback handlers (`_on_client_connect/_on_client_disconnect`), splitting connection lifecycle (register/unregister) between the transport and the server — overlapping responsibilities that make ownership of cleanup ambiguous.

WebSocket-specific settings `ws_host`/`ws_port` are passed to `PollingTransport`, which has no websocket semantics — a leaky abstraction that will force placeholder args or silent ignores when the polling transport is exercised.
`_create_transport` uses a string if/elif/else dispatch on the `TRANSPORT` env var; a registry/dict lookup would scale more cleanly as transport types grow.

The diff adds ~778 lines across 5 new files (two transport implementations plus a base) with no visible tests; the transport abstraction is the ideal seam for unit tests but none appear in the commit.

strengths: Introduces a clean pluggable transport abstraction (strategy pattern), decoupling `NotificationServer` from websockets-specific concerns and enabling polling as an alternative without touching business logic.
Consolidates broadcast and direct-message send paths into the transport, removing duplicated per-client gather/exception handling from the server.
Improves lifecycle management: transport runs as a cancellable task and `stop()` is awaited in the cleanup path, replacing the ad-hoc `ws_server.close()` block.
Preserves existing component interfaces (Message, ClientRegistry, RedisBroker, MessagePersistence, REST routes) and keeps the server's external API backward-compatible.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, debt-reducing refactor that cleanly abstracts the transport layer and improves shutdown handling; the measured convention score of 0.77 reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (__init__.py, app.py, client_registry.py, message_handler.py, example_usage.py), not this commit, which is itself convention-clean — hence the higher per-commit rating of 0.9.

problems.description: RateLimiter is imported and instantiated in NotificationServer but no enforcement is visible on the new /history endpoint (diff truncated, so confirm it is wired elsewhere; otherwise it is dead integration).
limit/offset are parsed with int() without try/except in _history_handler; a non-numeric query param raises an unhandled ValueError producing a 500.
The row-to-dict mapping block is duplicated across get_messages_chronological and get_messages_since; a shared _rows_to_messages helper would remove repetition.
cleanup_old_messages uses datetime.utcnow(), deprecated in Python 3.12; use datetime.now(timezone.utc).
API surface is inconsistent: get_messages_since and get_messages_count_since require channel while get_messages_chronological treats it as Optional.
Broad except that logs and returns []/0 masks real failures (matches existing class pattern but hides cleanup/storage errors from callers).

strengths: New methods follow the established MessagePersistence try/except + logger.error + empty-return pattern and single-query SQL style.
Well-designed pagination (limit+1 fetch for next-page detection, offset/limit params, capped at 1000) and chronological ordering.
TTL cleanup is a sensible cross-cutting concern, uses rowcount to report deletions, and is additive without breaking existing behavior.
History endpoint slots cleanly into the existing async handler + route-registration structure.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent cross-cutting session that adds a well-structured paginated history API and TTL cleanup while faithfully following existing persistence and route patterns, though unvalidated query parsing, a possibly unwired RateLimiter, and utcnow deprecation introduce modest debt (and the AST '+0 functions' measurement conflicts with the clearly visible new methods, so I weighted the diff's ground truth over that count).

compounding_issues: Seed codebase (app.py, a Flask todo API) was left untouched and unused in the final tree — dead code never integrated or removed.
Redis subscription overlaps: run() subscribes to both 'notifications:broadcast' and the 'notifications:*' pattern, so a broadcast publish matches both and can be delivered/duplicated twice.

WebSocket handler relies on the legacy websockets 2-positional-arg API (handle_client(ws, path) + deprecated WebSocketServerProtocol); safe only under the pinned websockets==13.0, with modernization risk on upgrade.
requirements.txt pins redis and flask in later sessions, but the notification server itself never uses flask — the extra dependency exists solely for the dead seed app.
Each persistence/REST call opens and closes a fresh sqlite connection (and queries build SQL with manual LIMIT/OFFSET), fine at demo scale but an early pattern that scales poorly.
key_decisions: S1: Greenfield build of a dedicated async notification server (aiohttp + websockets) with clean module seams (ClientRegistry, MessageHandler) instead of extending the unrelated Flask seed.
S2: Channel-based subscription model — subscribe/unsubscribe message types, per-channel routing, and channel-scoped REST endpoints.
S3: Redis pub/sub adopted as the multi-instance message backbone with a SQLite-backed MessagePersistence layer for history — infrastructure integration cleanly behind a service boundary.
S4: Abstract BaseTransport interface with env-var-selected WebSocket/Polling transports; REST API kept identical and all 54 tests passing unmodified — a disciplined, behavior-preserving refactor.
S5: Redis-counter rate limiting with graceful degradation (disabled when Redis is down), TTL-based message expiry background task, and a paginated chronological /history endpoint with has_more.
Each session self-verified with a growing pytest suite (31→41→54→54→73) and produced design docs (ARCHITECTURE.md, TRANSPORT_REFACTORING.md, IMPLEMENTATION_SUMMARY.md).
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and consistently across all five sessions. Session 1 stood up a complete, well-seamed core with 31 passing tests; Session 2 added channel features (41 tests); Session 3 integrated Redis pub/sub and SQLite persistence (54 tests); Session 4 was the standout — a behavior-preserving transport refactor that kept the API and test suite byte-for-byte intact (54 tests, zero changes); and Session 5 layered cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, history, TTL expiry) to reach 73 passing tests. The agent consistently verified with pytest after every change, documented each architectural shift, and never regressed the passing baseline, so the arc is a steady climb from solid foundation to feature-complete, well-tested system.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc (build core → add features → integrate infra → refactor → cross-cutting concerns) that improved quality each step with a growing, always-green test suite and disciplined behavior-preserving refactors.
